API.explanation: An API is an interface that lets different software applications communicate with each other
points: Acts as a contract between producer and consumer defining how requests and responses should work
Enables modularity, reusability, and integration across services, platforms, and organizations
Powers virtually every modern mobile app, web application, cloud service, and AI system
Can be public (open to anyone), partner (limited access), or private (internal only)
Proper design dramatically affects developer experience, security, scalability, and maintainability

REST API.explanation: REST APIs use standard HTTP methods to create, read, update, and delete web resources
points: Follows stateless, cacheable, uniform interface principles defined by Roy Fielding
Uses HTTP verbs (GET, POST, PUT, PATCH, DELETE) to perform CRUD operations on resources
Resources identified by URLs; responses typically in JSON (sometimes XML)
Most widely adopted API style due to simplicity, tooling support, and HTTP ecosystem
Common patterns include resource nesting, query params for filtering, and HATEOAS for discoverability

GraphQL.explanation: GraphQL lets clients request exactly the data they need in one flexible query
points: Single endpoint usually /graphql accepts complex, nested queries in POST body
Strongly typed schema with introspection enables powerful tooling and auto-completion
Eliminates over-fetching and under-fetching problems common in REST
Supports real-time updates via subscriptions over WebSockets
Batching, caching, and N+1 problem solutions (DataLoader) critical for performance

gRPC.explanation: gRPC is a high-performance RPC framework from Google using Protocol Buffers over HTTP/2
points: Uses binary Protocol Buffers for compact, efficient serialization
Supports four RPC types: unary, server streaming, client streaming, bidirectional
Built-in features: deadlines, cancellation, metadata, load balancing, authentication
Excellent for microservices, mobile clients, and low-latency internal communication
Code generation produces strongly-typed clients and servers in many languages

WebSocket.explanation: WebSockets provide persistent two-way communication channels between client and server
points: Upgrades from HTTP via handshake, then uses full-duplex binary/text frames
Ideal for real-time applications: chat, live updates, gaming, collaborative editing
Lower overhead than repeated HTTP polling or long-polling
Requires explicit connection management, heartbeats, and reconnection logic
Often secured with WSS (WebSocket Secure) using TLS

Webhook.explanation: Webhooks push real-time event data to your server URL when something happens in another app
points: Event-driven alternative to polling — server pushes updates instead of client asking
Common payload: JSON with event type, timestamp, data, and signature for verification
Requires public HTTPS endpoint, retry handling, and duplicate detection (idempotency)
Used extensively by Stripe, GitHub, Twilio, Shopify, Slack for notifications
Security best practice: verify HMAC signature using shared secret

HTTP Methods.explanation: GET, POST, PUT, PATCH, and DELETE are the HTTP verbs that define what an API request does
points: GET: retrieve resource (safe, idempotent, cacheable)
POST: create resource or trigger action (not idempotent)
PUT: replace entire resource (idempotent)
PATCH: partially update resource (idempotent when designed correctly)
DELETE: remove resource (idempotent)

Status Codes.explanation: HTTP status codes like 200, 404, and 500 tell the client what happened to its request
points: 2xx: success (200 OK, 201 Created, 204 No Content)
3xx: redirection (301 Moved Permanently, 304 Not Modified)
4xx: client error (400 Bad Request, 401 Unauthorized, 403 Forbidden, 404 Not Found, 429 Too Many Requests)
5xx: server error (500 Internal Server Error, 502 Bad Gateway, 503 Service Unavailable)
Consistent, semantic use of status codes dramatically improves debuggability

Authentication.explanation: API authentication verifies who is making a request using API keys, tokens, or OAuth
points: API Key: simple, good for server-to-server or low-risk public APIs
Bearer Token (JWT): stateless, contains claims, widely used with OAuth
OAuth 2.0: delegated authorization with access & refresh tokens
Mutual TLS: strong client + server identity verification via certificates
Best practice: never put credentials in URL; always use Authorization header

Rate Limiting.explanation: Rate limiting restricts how many API requests a client can make in a given time window
points: Common algorithms: token bucket, leaky bucket, fixed/sliding window
Protects against abuse, DDoS, cost explosion, and ensures fair usage
Usually enforced per API key, IP, or user account
Returns 429 Too Many Requests with Retry-After header
Advanced: per-endpoint, per-method, burst allowance, hierarchical limits

Endpoint.explanation: An API endpoint is a specific URL that represents a resource or action in the API
points: Follows RESTful conventions: /users, /users/{id}, /orders/{id}/items
Should be noun-centric (resources) rather than verb-centric
Versioning often in path (/v1/users), header, or subdomain
Consistent naming, pluralization, and hierarchy improve developer experience
Well-designed endpoints are intuitive, discoverable, and minimize client complexity

Request Body.explanation: The request body carries data sent to the API usually in JSON format for POST and PUT
points: Content-Type header must match payload (application/json most common)
Size limits typically enforced (1–10 MB common)
Validation should happen early (schema, required fields, format)
Large payloads often better handled via multipart or presigned URLs
Never log full request bodies containing sensitive data

Response Body.explanation: The response body contains the data the API returns after processing the request
points: Standard envelope pattern: { data, meta, errors } improves consistency
Errors should include code, message, details, and possibly retry info
Use consistent date/time format (ISO 8601) and numeric types
Pagination metadata (next, prev, total) critical for list endpoints
Minimize payload size for performance; use fields filtering when possible

Headers.explanation: HTTP headers pass metadata like content type, authorization tokens, and cache rules
points: Authorization: Bearer <token>, API key, Basic Auth
Content-Type / Accept: negotiate format (json, xml, etc.)
Cache-Control, ETag, Last-Modified: enable efficient caching
X-Request-ID / Correlation-ID: enable distributed tracing
Custom headers should use X- prefix or register official ones

Query Parameters.explanation: Query parameters are key-value pairs appended to URLs to filter or customize API responses
points: Common uses: filtering (?status=active), sorting (?sort=-created_at), pagination (?page=2&limit=50)
Should be optional and have sensible defaults
Arrays often repeated (?tag=urgent&tag=bug) or comma-separated
Sensitive data should never go in query strings (logged in servers, visible in URLs)
Excessive query params can make URLs hard to read — prefer body for complex filters

Path Parameters.explanation: Path parameters are variable parts of the URL that identify specific resources
points: Common pattern: /users/{userId}, /orders/{orderId}/items/{itemId}
Usually mapped to URL segments via framework routing
Should be required and uniquely identify the resource
Validation (format, existence) should happen early
Keep paths clean and hierarchical for readability

Pagination.explanation: Pagination splits large API responses into pages to avoid returning too much data at once
points: Styles: offset/limit (?page=1&limit=20), cursor-based (?after=abc123)
Cursor / keyset pagination better for large datasets and stable sorting
Include total count, next/previous links, or cursors in response
Default limit usually 20–100; allow higher with caution
Inconsistent pagination causes poor developer experience and performance issues

OAuth 2.0.explanation: OAuth 2.0 lets users authorize apps to access their data without sharing passwords
points: Grant types: authorization code (most secure), PKCE (SPAs), client credentials (machine-to-machine)
Tokens: access token (short-lived), refresh token (long-lived)
Scopes define granular permissions (read:profile, write:posts)
OpenID Connect extends OAuth for authentication (ID token)
Authorization server, resource server, client roles clearly separated

JWT.explanation: JSON Web Tokens are compact signed tokens used to securely transmit authentication claims
points: Three parts: header.payload.signature (base64url encoded)
Can be stateless (no session lookup) when properly signed/verified
Claims: iss, sub, aud, exp, nbf, iat, jti, custom data
Never put sensitive data in payload — it's only base64, not encrypted
Refresh tokens should be opaque and stored server-side for security

API Key.explanation: API keys are simple secret strings that authenticate clients making requests to an API
points: Usually long random strings passed in header (X-API-Key) or query (?api_key=…)
Good for server-to-server communication or public read-only APIs
Should be rotatable, revocable, and scoped to specific permissions
Never commit to git or expose in client-side code
Rate limiting and usage quotas almost always tied to API keys

HTTPS.explanation: HTTPS encrypts all data between client and server so it cannot be intercepted
points: HTTP + TLS/SSL encryption layer
Prevents man-in-the-middle attacks, eavesdropping, tampering
Modern requirement: all public APIs must use HTTPS
HSTS header forces browsers to always use HTTPS
Free certificates available via Let's Encrypt since 2015

TLS.explanation: TLS is the encryption protocol that secures HTTPS connections between client and server
points: Current recommended version: TLS 1.3 (faster, more secure)
TLS 1.0/1.1 deprecated; TLS 1.2 still widely supported but phasing out
Strong ciphers, forward secrecy, and certificate validation essential
Mutual TLS (mTLS) authenticates both client and server
Certificate management, rotation, and revocation critical for security

CORS.explanation: CORS controls which web origins are allowed to make requests to your API
points: Browser security feature preventing cross-origin requests by default
Key headers: Access-Control-Allow-Origin, Allow-Methods, Allow-Headers, Allow-Credentials
Preflight (OPTIONS) request required for non-simple requests
Wildcard (*) allowed only without credentials
Misconfigured CORS is a frequent cause of frontend API errors

JSON.explanation: JSON is the universal lightweight data format for sending structured data between systems
points: Simple, human-readable, language-independent
Native support in virtually every programming language
Numbers, strings, booleans, arrays, objects, null
Standard date format: ISO 8601 strings (not native Date type)
Large numbers may lose precision (use strings for IDs, money)

XML.explanation: XML is an older structured data format used in legacy APIs and enterprise systems
points: Verbose, schema-capable (XSD), namespace support
Still used in SOAP, SAML, RSS, some financial/healthcare systems
Larger payloads and slower parsing compared to JSON
XPath, XSLT, XML namespaces add power but complexity
Most modern APIs prefer JSON unless legacy compatibility required

Protocol Buffers.explanation: Protobuf is Google's binary serialization format much smaller and faster than JSON
points: Schema-first (.proto files) → generates code in many languages
Backward and forward compatible field evolution
Used heavily in gRPC, internal microservices, mobile apps
5–10× smaller and 5–10× faster than equivalent JSON
Binary format → not human-readable without tools

OpenAPI Spec.explanation: OpenAPI is the standard specification for documenting RESTful APIs in a machine-readable format
points: Formerly Swagger 2.0; current version OpenAPI 3.0 / 3.1
YAML or JSON document describing paths, operations, parameters, schemas
Enables auto-generated docs (Swagger UI), client SDKs, server stubs, validation
Industry standard supported by almost every API framework
OpenAPI Generator creates clients in 50+ languages from spec

Swagger.explanation: Swagger tools generate interactive API documentation and client SDKs from OpenAPI specs
points: Swagger UI: interactive documentation interface
Swagger Codegen / OpenAPI Generator: client & server code generation
Swagger Editor: visual editor for OpenAPI specs
Integrated into Spring Boot, FastAPI, NestJS, Go, etc.
Try-it-out feature lets developers test endpoints directly

API Gateway.explanation: An API gateway is a single entry point that routes requests, handles auth, and manages traffic
points: Popular solutions: AWS API Gateway, Kong, Apigee, Tyk, Traefik, Zuul
Handles authentication, rate limiting, caching, request transformation
Routes to multiple backend microservices
Central place for monitoring, logging, and analytics
Can add latency; must be highly available and performant

Reverse Proxy.explanation: A reverse proxy sits in front of servers to handle routing, load balancing, and security
points: Popular: NGINX, HAProxy, Traefik, Envoy, Caddy
Terminates TLS, compresses responses, serves static files
Hides backend server details from clients
Can cache responses, rewrite URLs, add headers
Essential component in most production API deployments

Load Balancer.explanation: A load balancer distributes incoming API requests across multiple servers for reliability
points: Algorithms: round-robin, least connections, IP hash, consistent hashing
Layers: L4 (TCP) vs L7 (HTTP/HTTPS)
Health checks ensure only healthy instances receive traffic
Cloud-native: AWS ALB/NLB/ELB, GCP Load Balancer, Azure Load Balancer
Critical for horizontal scaling and high availability

Caching.explanation: API response caching stores results so repeated identical requests are served instantly
points: Levels: CDN (Cloudflare, Akamai), gateway, in-memory (Redis), HTTP cache headers
Cache-Control, ETag, Last-Modified guide client & intermediary caching
Cache invalidation remains one of the hardest problems in computer science
Cache key design critical (include all variable params, headers)
Cache-aside, read-through, write-through patterns common

Idempotency.explanation: An idempotent API call can be safely repeated multiple times without different side effects
points: GET, PUT, DELETE, PATCH usually idempotent by design
POST often not idempotent (creates new resource each time)
Idempotency-Key header pattern for safe retries on non-idempotent operations
Critical for payments, order creation, user signup
Server stores key + result for short period to return same response

Versioning.explanation: API versioning lets you update your API without breaking existing clients using the old version
points: Common approaches: URL path (/v1/), header (Accept: application/vnd.myapi.v2+json), query param
Semantic versioning (SemVer) for major/minor/patch changes
Date-based versioning (2024-03-01) used by Stripe, Twilio
Avoid forever support of old versions — use deprecation periods
Good versioning strategy reduces client migration pain

Deprecation.explanation: API deprecation signals that an endpoint will be removed giving developers time to migrate
points: Use Deprecation header or sunset date in response
Typical timeline: announce → 6–12 months → block → remove
Communicate via developer portal, email, changelog
Provide migration guides and replacement endpoints
Monitor usage of deprecated endpoints to plan sunset

Throttling.explanation: Throttling slows down or blocks API requests that exceed defined usage limits
points: Different from rate limiting — can dynamically slow responses instead of hard block
Used during overload to protect backend while giving fair access
429 + Retry-After header signals client to slow down
Can be combined with queueing for burst tolerance
Essential for public APIs with unpredictable traffic

Circuit Breaker.explanation: A circuit breaker stops calling a failing API temporarily to prevent cascading failures
points: States: closed (normal), open (fail fast), half-open (test recovery)
Popular libraries: Resilience4j, Polly, Hystrix (legacy)
Prevents overwhelming failing downstream service
Usually combined with fallback, timeout, and retry
Critical pattern in microservices architectures

Retry Logic.explanation: Retry logic automatically resends failed API requests with exponential backoff
points: Exponential backoff + jitter prevents thundering herd
Classify errors: retryable (429, 503) vs non-retryable (400, 401)
Max attempts, total timeout, per-attempt timeout
Idempotency key required for safe retries on mutating calls
Client-side resilience pattern that dramatically improves reliability

Timeout.explanation: API timeouts cancel requests that take too long to prevent hanging indefinitely
points: Client timeout < server timeout < gateway timeout
Typical values: 5–30 seconds for most APIs
Always set connect timeout separately from read timeout
504 Gateway Timeout when upstream times out
Timeouts are the most common cause of cascading failures

SDK.explanation: An SDK is a pre-built library in your language that makes calling an API much easier
points: Generated from OpenAPI spec or hand-written for better ergonomics
Handles auth, retries, pagination, error parsing, request signing
Official SDKs usually exist for JavaScript, Python, Java, Go, .NET, etc.
Greatly improves developer experience and reduces bugs
Should be versioned alongside API and well-documented

Postman.explanation: Postman is the most popular tool for testing, documenting, and collaborating on APIs
points: Collections shareable via links or workspaces
Environments for dev/staging/prod variables
Mock servers, monitors, Newman CLI for CI/CD
Supports REST, GraphQL, WebSocket, gRPC
Team collaboration features in paid plans

Insomnia.explanation: Insomnia is a REST and GraphQL API testing client with a clean developer-friendly interface
points: Open-source core with paid enterprise features
Excellent GraphQL support including schema introspection
Environments, git sync, plugin ecosystem
Lightweight alternative to Postman
Strong focus on design-first workflows

cURL.explanation: cURL is a command-line tool for making HTTP requests to test APIs from the terminal
points: Universal availability on Linux, macOS, Windows (via Git Bash)
Supports all HTTP methods, headers, JSON bodies, auth types
Verbose mode (-v) shows full request/response for debugging
Scriptable — foundation of many API testing scripts
Postman can export requests as cURL commands

Mock API.explanation: Mock APIs simulate real API responses so frontend development can proceed without a backend
points: Tools: Mockoon, WireMock, json-server, Prism, Beeceptor
Define expected responses, delays, status codes, dynamic data
Critical for parallel frontend/backend development
Can use OpenAPI spec to generate realistic mocks
Also useful for demoing, testing edge cases, CI

API Contract.explanation: An API contract is the agreed specification of inputs, outputs, and behavior between teams
points: Usually OpenAPI/AsyncAPI document or Protobuf schema
Enables parallel development, contract testing, documentation
Consumer-driven contracts (CDC) let consumers define expectations
Versioned and reviewed like code
Reduces integration surprises and rework

Consumer-driven Contracts.explanation: Consumer-driven contracts let API consumers define the exact responses they need from providers
points: Tools: Pact, Spring Cloud Contract, Schemathesis
Consumers write tests → generate contract → provider verifies
Ensures provider doesn't break consumer expectations
Particularly valuable in microservices with independent teams
Reduces integration test flakiness

API Testing.explanation: API testing validates that endpoints return correct responses for valid and invalid inputs
points: Unit (individual endpoint), integration (multiple services), contract, security, performance
Tools: Postman/Newman, RestAssured, Supertest, Karate, Dredd
Test happy path, error cases, edge cases, auth failures
Schema validation + response assertions critical
Run in CI/CD pipeline for regression protection

Integration Testing.explanation: Integration tests verify that multiple services work correctly together end-to-end
points: Test real network calls between services (not mocks)
Usually slower and more brittle than unit tests
Use test doubles for external systems (payment, email)
Contract tests can reduce need for full integration tests
Run less frequently than unit tests in CI

Load Testing.explanation: Load testing simulates high traffic to find how much a system can handle before degrading
points: Tools: k6, Locust, JMeter, Gatling, Artillery
Measure throughput, latency (p50, p95, p99), error rate
Ramp-up, steady state, spike, soak tests
Identify bottlenecks: DB, CPU, memory, network, locks
Should be part of performance budget in CI/CD

Chaos Engineering.explanation: Chaos engineering deliberately breaks things to find weaknesses before real failures occur
points: Principles from Netflix Chaos Monkey family
Tools: Chaos Mesh, LitmusChaos, Gremlin, PowerfulSeal
Common experiments: kill pods, delay network, CPU/memory stress, partition
Blast radius control and rollback critical
Builds confidence in system resilience

Service Mesh.explanation: A service mesh handles service-to-service communication, security, and observability automatically
points: Popular: Istio, Linkerd, Consul Connect, AWS App Mesh
Sidecar proxies (Envoy) per service
mTLS, traffic shifting, circuit breaking, retries, observability all automatic
Greatly reduces boilerplate in microservices
Adds latency and complexity — weigh benefits carefully

Microservices.explanation: Microservices split a large app into small independent services that communicate over APIs
points: Benefits: independent scaling, technology choice, team autonomy, resilience
Challenges: distributed complexity, data consistency, observability, deployment coordination
Usually deployed with containers + orchestration (Kubernetes)
API gateway or service mesh almost always required
Not always better than well-modularized monolith

Monolith.explanation: A monolith is a single large application where all components are deployed together
points: Simpler development, debugging, deployment, and transactions
Easier refactoring across modules
Scaling requires replicating entire app
Modern monoliths can be modular and highly maintainable
Many successful companies start as monolith and split later (monolith-first)

Event-driven API.explanation: Event-driven APIs emit events when things change letting subscribers react in real time
points: Usually use webhooks, message queues (Kafka, RabbitMQ), or pub/sub (Google Pub/Sub)
Decouples producers and consumers
Enables reactive, scalable architectures
Requires reliable delivery, ordering guarantees, idempotency
AsyncAPI specification standardizing documentation

Server-Sent Events.explanation: SSE lets servers push updates to clients over a single persistent HTTP connection
points: Simpler than WebSocket for unidirectional push
Text-based event stream format
Auto-reconnect built into browsers
Good for live feeds, notifications, stock prices
Less flexible than WebSocket (no client→server messages)

Long Polling.explanation: Long polling holds a request open until the server has new data to send back
points: Fallback when WebSocket/SSE not available
Higher resource usage than WebSocket
Requires careful timeout and reconnection logic
Used in older chat systems and legacy apps
Mostly replaced by modern real-time protocols

SOAP.explanation: SOAP is an older XML-based API protocol still used in legacy enterprise systems
points: Envelope with header + body, WSDL contract
Built-in security (WS-Security), transactions, reliable messaging
Very verbose and complex compared to REST/JSON
Still common in banking, government, healthcare
Modern replacements: REST or gRPC preferred

RPC.explanation: Remote Procedure Call lets you call a function on a remote server as if it were local
points: gRPC is modern, high-performance RPC
Older: XML-RPC, JSON-RPC, Thrift
Procedure-oriented rather than resource-oriented (unlike REST)
Strong typing and code generation common
Good for internal services where performance matters

Serialization.explanation: Serialization converts objects into a transmittable format like JSON or binary for API calls
points: Formats: JSON, XML, Protobuf, Avro, MessagePack, CBOR
Trade-offs: human readability vs size vs speed vs schema evolution
Date/time, big integers, enums need careful handling
Security: never deserialize untrusted data without validation
Performance bottleneck in high-throughput APIs

Deserialization.explanation: Deserialization converts received bytes or JSON back into a usable object in memory
points: Vulnerable to injection attacks if not done safely
Use schema validation before full deserialization
Known issues: Java ObjectInputStream, PHP unserialize, YAML !! tags
Safe libraries: Jackson, Gson, msgpack, Protobuf
Always validate and sanitize untrusted input

Content Negotiation.explanation: Content negotiation lets clients specify what format they want the API to return
points: Via Accept header (application/json, application/xml)
Server responds with Content-Type
Quality factors (q=0.8) allow preference ordering
Fallback to default format if no match
Less common today — most APIs are JSON-only

HATEOAS.explanation: HATEOAS includes links in API responses guiding clients on what actions they can take next
points: Hypermedia as the Engine of Application State — REST maturity level 3
Example: { "order": {...}, "_links": { "pay": { "href": "/orders/123/pay" }}}
Enables discoverable, self-documenting APIs
Rarely fully implemented due to complexity
Tools: Spring HATEOAS, HAL, JSON API specification

API Composition.explanation: API composition aggregates data from multiple microservices into a single response
points: Patterns: server-side aggregation, BFF (Backend for Frontend), GraphQL federation
Reduces client round-trips and complexity
Can become performance bottleneck if not cached
Error handling and partial failures need careful design
Popular in e-commerce, dashboards, mobile apps

BFF Pattern.explanation: Backend for Frontend creates a dedicated API tailored to each client type like mobile or web
points: One BFF per client type (web, iOS, Android, partner)
Aggregates, transforms, and optimizes data for specific UI needs
Reduces client complexity and over-fetching
Owned by frontend team in some organizations
Can lead to code duplication if not managed carefully

API Monetization.explanation: API monetization charges developers for usage enabling APIs to be a revenue stream
points: Models: freemium, pay-per-call, subscription tiers, revenue share
Stripe Billing, Zuora, RapidAPI marketplace common platforms
Usage metering: per request, per compute unit, per data volume
Developer experience critical for adoption
Requires strong analytics, billing integration, and support

Developer Portal.explanation: A developer portal provides API docs, sandbox, and key management for external developers
points: Popular platforms: Redocly, Stoplight, ReadMe, Bump.sh, Backstage
Features: interactive docs, API console, usage dashboard, forums
Self-service onboarding and key provisioning
SEO-optimized landing page for discoverability
Analytics on which docs are most viewed

Sandbox.explanation: An API sandbox is a test environment where developers can experiment without real-world consequences
points: Separate base URL, test credentials, fake data
No real charges, emails, or side effects
Often pre-populated with sample data
Critical for safe experimentation and demos
Should mirror production as closely as possible

Webhook Retry.explanation: Webhook retry logic resends failed event deliveries with backoff to ensure no data is lost
points: Typical: exponential backoff, max attempts (5–10), dead-letter queue
Respect HTTP status codes (429 → longer delay)
Idempotency key in payload prevents duplicates
Monitor delivery success rate
Many platforms (Stripe, SendGrid) provide configurable retry rules

Idempotency Key.explanation: An idempotency key lets clients safely retry API requests without creating duplicate operations
points: Client generates unique key per operation
Server stores key + response for short period (24h common)
Returns same response for same key
Essential for payments, order creation, transfers
Stripe, PayPal, Square use this pattern

API Latency.explanation: API latency is the time from sending a request to receiving the first byte of response
points: Includes network RTT + server processing time
Measured at p50, p95, p99 percentiles
Typical good values: <100ms p50, <500ms p99 for most APIs
Affected by geography, cold starts, DB queries, external calls
Critical UX factor for mobile and interactive apps

P99 Latency.explanation: P99 latency is the response time that 99 percent of requests complete within
points: Tail latency — focuses on worst 1% of requests
Much more important than average for user experience
Outliers often caused by GC pauses, slow DB queries, network blips
Goal: keep p99 under 1–2 seconds for most APIs
Requires careful monitoring and chaos testing

SLA.explanation: A Service Level Agreement guarantees minimum API uptime and performance metrics to customers
points: Typical: 99.9% uptime (“three nines”), 500ms p95 latency
Includes error budget concept
Violations trigger credits or refunds
Separate internal SLOs stricter than external SLA
Requires robust monitoring and alerting

Uptime.explanation: Uptime is the percentage of time an API is available and responding correctly
points: Calculated as (total time – downtime) / total time × 100
Five nines (99.999%) ≈ 5 minutes downtime/year
Measured via synthetic monitoring (uptime checks)
Includes planned maintenance if not communicated
Public status page shows current/historical uptime

Zero Downtime Deploy.explanation: Zero downtime deployment updates the API without dropping any requests from clients
points: Strategies: blue-green, rolling updates, canary releases
Requires backward-compatible changes or feature flags
Health checks and readiness probes essential
Kubernetes, ECS, Nomad support native rolling updates
Goal for high-availability services

Blue-Green Deployment.explanation: Blue-green deploys a new API version alongside the old one then switches traffic instantly
points: Blue = live, green = new version
Instant rollback by switching back to blue
Requires double capacity during deployment
DNS or load balancer switchover
Popular in cloud environments with auto-scaling groups

Canary Release.explanation: A canary release routes a small percentage of traffic to a new API version first
points: Monitor metrics before full rollout
Easy rollback by shifting traffic back
Supported natively by Istio, Flagger, Kubernetes
Reduces blast radius of bad releases

Feature Flags.explanation: Feature flags turn API features on or off without deploying new code
points: Tools: LaunchDarkly, Unleash, Flagsmith, ConfigCat
Granular targeting: user, percentage, region, environment
Enables dark launches, A/B testing, kill switches
Critical for safe continuous deployment
Must clean up old flags to avoid technical debt

API Observability.explanation: API observability tracks logs, metrics, and traces to understand how your API behaves in production
points: Three pillars: logs (what happened), metrics (how much), traces (how long, where)
Tools: Prometheus + Grafana, Datadog, New Relic, Honeycomb, OpenTelemetry
Golden signals: latency, traffic, errors, saturation
Structured logging (JSON) with correlation IDs
Enables proactive alerting and debugging

Distributed Tracing.explanation: Distributed tracing follows a request across multiple services to pinpoint where it slows down
points: Span = unit of work; trace = end-to-end request
Context propagation via headers (Traceparent, B3, W3C)
OpenTelemetry standard unifying Jaeger, Zipkin, etc.
Critical for microservices debugging
Sampling strategies needed at scale

API Security.explanation: API security protects against injection, broken auth, excessive data exposure, and DDoS attacks
points: OWASP API Security Top 10 primary reference
Defense in depth: auth, input validation, rate limiting, WAF
Never trust client input — validate everything
Regular security audits and penetration testing
Security must be part of design, not bolt-on

OWASP API Top 10.explanation: OWASP API Top 10 lists the most critical API security risks developers must protect against
points: 2023 version: Broken Object Level Authorization #1
Excessive Data Exposure, Mass Assignment, Injection still major
Broken Authentication, Security Misconfiguration, Improper Assets Management
Updated regularly based on real-world data
Primary checklist for API security reviews

Mutual TLS.explanation: Mutual TLS requires both client and server to present certificates proving their identity
points: Strongest form of API authentication for machine-to-machine
No shared secrets — cryptographic identity
Certificate rotation and revocation required
Common in financial services, healthcare, government
Harder to manage at scale than token auth

API Analytics.explanation: API analytics track usage patterns, popular endpoints, and error rates for business insights
points: Measure adoption, growth, top consumers, error trends
Tools: Moesif, Google Analytics for APIs, Datadog API monitoring
Helps prioritize features, detect abuse, plan capacity
Segment by key, app, developer, geography
Critical for monetized and partner APIs

AsyncAPI.explanation: AsyncAPI is a specification standard for documenting event-driven and message-based APIs
points: Similar to OpenAPI but for async protocols (Kafka, MQTT, AMQP, WebSocket)
Describes channels, messages, schemas, security
Generates docs, code, tests similar to OpenAPI
Growing adoption for event-driven architectures
AsyncAPI Initiative community-driven

GraphQL Subscription.explanation: GraphQL subscriptions use WebSockets to push real-time updates when data changes
points: subscription { messageAdded(channelId: "1") { text } }
Server maintains WebSocket connection per client
Pub/sub pattern under the hood (Redis, Kafka, in-memory)
Authentication and authorization per subscription
Backpressure and connection limits important

DataLoader.explanation: DataLoader batches and caches GraphQL data fetches to prevent N+1 query performance issues
points: Created by Facebook for GraphQL-js
Batches identical requests in same tick
Caches results within single request
Essential for relational data in GraphQL
Available in most GraphQL server libraries

Federation.explanation: GraphQL federation combines multiple independent GraphQL APIs into one unified schema
points: Apollo Federation most popular implementation
Each service defines its part of graph with @key, @extends
Gateway stitches schemas and routes queries
Enables microservices-style GraphQL
Schema composition and ownership challenges

Introspection.explanation: GraphQL introspection lets clients query the schema to discover available types and operations
points: __schema and __type special fields
Powers GraphiQL, Playground, auto-completion
Can be disabled in production for security
Introspection query size can be large
Used by codegen tools for type-safe clients

Field Resolvers.explanation: GraphQL field resolvers are functions that fetch or compute the value of each schema field
points: Root resolver → field resolvers → nested resolvers
Can be sync or async
Context, args, info parameters available
Place for auth checks, data loading, business logic
Performance bottleneck if N+1 not handled

API Governance.explanation: API governance enforces standards, naming conventions, and security policies across all APIs
points: Style guides, naming conventions, error formats
Linting of OpenAPI specs (Spectral, vacuum)
Review process for new APIs and major changes
Central catalog/discovery of all APIs
Balances consistency with team autonomy

Streaming API.explanation: Streaming APIs send data incrementally as it becomes available instead of waiting for the full response
points: Transfer-Encoding: chunked or gRPC streaming
Good for large datasets, logs, video, search-as-you-type
Client must handle partial responses
Backpressure support important
HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 improve streaming efficiency

Batch API.explanation: Batch APIs accept many requests in one call to reduce round trips and improve throughput
points: Example: Google Batch API, JSON-RPC batch
Single response with array of results or errors
Partial success handling critical
Greatly reduces latency for mobile clients
Size limits and individual request timeouts apply

API Composition Pattern.explanation: API composition aggregates multiple microservice calls into one response on the server side
points: Reduces client-side orchestration
Can be done in gateway, dedicated composition service, or BFF
Caching and parallel fetching important for performance
Error propagation and partial responses need design
Common in e-commerce product detail pages

Back-pressure.explanation: Back-pressure signals an overwhelmed API to slow down the rate incoming requests are sent
points: Reactive Streams, gRPC flow control, HTTP/2 flow control
Prevents memory exhaustion and cascading failures
Better than dropping requests or 503
Requires client cooperation
Essential in streaming and high-throughput systems

API Deprecation Policy.explanation: A deprecation policy gives developers adequate notice and migration time before removing API features
points: Typical: 6–12 months notice for breaking changes
Announce via changelog, email, developer portal
Provide migration guides and tools
Monitor usage to identify affected clients
Sunset date after which access is blocked

Contract Testing.explanation: Contract tests verify both API provider and consumer honor the agreed schema and behavior
points: Pact, Spring Cloud Contract, Dredd, Schemathesis
Consumer publishes expected contract → provider verifies
Catches breaking changes early
Reduces need for heavy integration tests
Works well with CI/CD pipelines

API Schema Validation.explanation: Schema validation automatically rejects requests that do not conform to the API specification
points: OpenAPI → validate request/response against spec
Tools: express-openapi-validator, swagger-validator, spectral
Early rejection saves processing time
Better error messages than runtime failures
Can be strict or lenient depending on stage

Optimistic UI.explanation: Optimistic UI assumes API calls succeed and updates the interface before getting confirmation
points: Greatly improves perceived performance
Rollback on failure with error message
Used by Twitter/X, GitHub, Figma, Notion
Requires conflict resolution strategy
Pair with undo stack for best experience

API Portal.explanation: An API portal provides documentation, sandbox testing, key management, and usage analytics
points: Often built on top of OpenAPI spec
Self-service onboarding experience
Showcases use cases, tutorials, code samples
Usage dashboard for developers
Critical for public and partner APIs

Webhook Security.explanation: Webhook security verifies delivery authenticity using HMAC signatures on the payload
points: HMAC-SHA256 of payload with shared secret
Timestamp in signature prevents replay attacks
Verify before processing payload
Standard practice by Stripe, GitHub, Twilio
Reject unsigned or invalid signature immediately
